```{r load-hotel-data, include = FALSE}
hotel_data <- read_csv("H2.csv", na = c("NULL", "NA", ""), trim_ws = TRUE)
```

```{r load-weather-data, include = FALSE}
weather_cache_path <- "weather_raw.rds"

if (file.exists(weather_cache_path)) {
  weather_raw <- readRDS(weather_cache_path)
} else {
  url <- paste0(
    "https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive",
    "?latitude=38.72&longitude=-9.13",
    "&start_date=2015-01-01&end_date=2017-12-31",
    "&daily=temperature_2m_mean,precipitation_sum,sunshine_duration",
    "&timezone=Europe/Lisbon"
  )
  response    <- GET(url)
  weather_raw <- fromJSON(content(response, "text", encoding = "UTF-8"))
  saveRDS(weather_raw, weather_cache_path)
}

weather_daily <- as_tibble(weather_raw$daily) |>
  mutate(time = as.Date(time))

weather_monthly <- weather_daily |>
  mutate(
    year  = year(time),
    month = month.name[month(time)]
  ) |>
  group_by(year, month) |>
  summarise(
    avg_temp_c       = mean(temperature_2m_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
    precipitation_mm = sum(precipitation_sum,    na.rm = TRUE),
    sunshine_hours   = sum(sunshine_duration,    na.rm = TRUE) / 3600,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

hotel_data <- hotel_data %>%
  left_join(weather_monthly,
            by = c("ArrivalDateYear" = "year",
                   "ArrivalDateMonth" = "month"))
```

```{r preprocessing, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
hotel_data <- hotel_data %>%
  mutate(
    across(where(is.character), trimws),
    Agent   = ifelse(Agent   %in% c("NULL", ""), NA, Agent),
    Company = ifelse(Company %in% c("NULL", ""), NA, Company),
    total_stays = StaysInWeekendNights + StaysInWeekNights,
    arrival_season = case_when(
      ArrivalDateMonth %in% c("March", "April", "May")            ~ "Spring",
      ArrivalDateMonth %in% c("June", "July", "August")           ~ "Summer",
      ArrivalDateMonth %in% c("September", "October", "November") ~ "Autumn",
      TRUE                                                          ~ "Winter"
    ),
    is_via_agent = ifelse(is.na(Agent), 0L, 1L),
    country_region = case_when(
      Country %in% c("PRT","ESP","FRA","ITA","DEU","BEL",
                     "NLD","CHE","AUT","LUX","AND")               ~ "Western Europe",
      Country %in% c("GBR","IRL","DNK","SWE","NOR","FIN",
                     "ISL","POL","CZE","SVK","HUN")               ~ "N/E Europe",
      Country %in% c("USA","CAN","BRA","ARG","MEX","COL")         ~ "Americas",
      TRUE                                                          ~ "Other"
    ),
    Children = ifelse(is.na(Children), 0, Children)
  )

hotel_data <- hotel_data[, setdiff(names(hotel_data),
                          c("ReservationStatus", "ReservationStatusDate", "Company"))]

hotel_data <- hotel_data %>%
  mutate(
    MarketSegment    = relevel(factor(MarketSegment),  ref = "Online TA"),
    CustomerType     = relevel(factor(CustomerType),   ref = "Transient"),
    DepositType      = relevel(factor(DepositType),    ref = "No Deposit"),
    Meal             = relevel(factor(Meal),           ref = "BB"),
    arrival_season   = relevel(factor(arrival_season), ref = "Summer"),
    country_region   = relevel(factor(country_region), ref = "Western Europe"),
    ReservedRoomType = factor(ReservedRoomType),
    IsCanceled       = as.integer(IsCanceled),
    IsRepeatedGuest  = as.integer(IsRepeatedGuest)
  )

mean_lt   <- round(mean(hotel_data$LeadTime), 1)
mean_temp <- round(mean(hotel_data$avg_temp_c, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

cat("Dataset ready:", nrow(hotel_data), "bookings,", ncol(hotel_data), "variables\n")
```

---

# Introduction

A hotel room unsold tonight is revenue gone forever. Unlike a retailer who can sell yesterday's inventory today, a hotel cannot recover a night that passed empty. This makes forecasting — of price, of stay length, of cancellations — not a nice-to-have but an operational necessity.

This report analyses **79,330 booking records** from a single city hotel in Lisbon, Portugal, covering reservations made between July 2015 and August 2017. The data were published by Antonio, Almeida, and Nunes (2019) and capture the full lifecycle of each booking: when it was made, who made it, what was requested, what was paid, and whether the guest ultimately arrived. Monthly weather observations for Lisbon — temperature, precipitation, and sunshine hours — from the Open-Meteo historical archive are joined as complementary predictors.

Three questions drive the analysis, each with direct operational stakes:

> **RQ1 — Price:** Which booking and seasonal characteristics determine the average daily rate a guest pays?

> **RQ2 — Stay length:** Which guest segments book the longest stays, and by how much?

> **RQ3 — Cancellation:** What information available at booking time most reliably predicts whether a reservation will be cancelled?

## Research Questions and Modelling Strategy

Six models address these questions. RQ1 and RQ2 each warrant a single well-specified parametric model: the response variables are continuous and count-valued respectively, and the relationships involved are well-described by additive structure on the appropriate transformed scale. RQ3 is approached through four models of increasing flexibility, because cancellation risk is the highest-stakes prediction problem and the one most likely to contain nonlinear and interactive structure that simpler models miss.

```{r modelling-ladder, echo = FALSE}
ladder_df <- data.frame(
  Model = c(
    "Model 1 — Linear Model",
    "Model 2 — Poisson GLM",
    "Model 3 — Binomial GLM",
    "Model 4 — GAM",
    "Model 5 — SVM (linear & RBF kernel)",
    "Model 6 — Neural Network"
  ),
  RQ = c("RQ1 — Price", "RQ2 — Stay length",
         "RQ3 — Cancellation", "RQ3 — Cancellation",
         "RQ3 — Cancellation", "RQ3 — Cancellation"),
  Rationale = c(
    "log(ADR) is approximately Gaussian; coefficients are multiplicative percentage effects on price — the language revenue managers use.",
    "total_stays is a non-negative integer count; Poisson GLM guarantees non-negative predictions and produces rate ratios. Overdispersion is tested and corrected if present.",
    "Linear log-odds baseline. Coefficients are odds ratios — interpretable and directly actionable. Establishes which predictors matter and in which direction.",
    "Replaces linear terms for three continuous predictors with penalised splines. Each smooth's effective degrees of freedom (EDF) quantifies how nonlinear the relationship truly is.",
    "The RBF kernel can represent arbitrary nonlinear decision boundaries and feature interactions. The linear kernel serves as an explicit control: any AUC gap between the two kernels isolates the contribution of nonlinearity from differences in fitting principle.",
    "Hidden units learn their own basis functions end-to-end. The most flexible model in the report; permutation importance reveals which predictors the network uses differently from the GLM."
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

kable(ladder_df,
      caption = "Table 0: Six models across three research questions. Models 3–6 form a deliberate ladder: each step removes one specific assumption made by the step above, so the AUC gain at each rung has a clean methodological interpretation.",
      col.names = c("Model", "Research Question", "Rationale & what it adds"),
      align = c("l", "l", "l")) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = TRUE, font_size = 11,
                bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) %>%
  column_spec(1, width = "22%", bold = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "16%") %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "62%")
```

All models are trained on held-out splits and evaluated on unseen test data. For the four cancellation models, the split is identical — any difference in test-set performance reflects the model class, not the data each model had access to.

# Exploratory Data Analysis

Good analysis begins with honest description. This section examines what the dataset contains, what patterns emerge without any modelling assumptions, and what data quality issues require attention. Every preprocessing and modelling decision in the sections that follow traces back to a finding here.

## The Data at a Glance

```{r eda-snapshot, echo = FALSE}
snapshot <- data.frame(
  Area = c("Who booked", "How it was booked", "What was booked",
           "What happened", "When they arrived", "Weather context"),
  Key_Variables = c(
    "CustomerType, Country, Adults, Children, IsRepeatedGuest",
    "MarketSegment, DistributionChannel, Agent, LeadTime, DepositType",
    "ReservedRoomType, Meal, TotalOfSpecialRequests, RequiredCarParkingSpaces",
    "IsCanceled, ADR, StaysInWeekendNights, StaysInWeekNights",
    "ArrivalDateYear, ArrivalDateMonth, arrival_season",
    "avg_temp_c, precipitation_mm, sunshine_hours"
  ),
  Notes = c(
    "74.9% Transient; 39% from Portugal",
    "48.9% Online TA; median lead time 74 days",
    "BB meal plan = 78.5% of bookings",
    "41.7% cancelled; median ADR €100",
    "2015–2017; August is busiest month",
    "Joined from Open-Meteo API on arrival month"
  )
)

kable(snapshot,
      caption = "Table 1: Dataset structure — 79,330 bookings, 31 variables across six areas.",
      col.names = c("Area", "Key Variables", "Notable Facts")) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = TRUE, font_size = 11) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
```

Three variables are excluded before any model is fitted. `ReservationStatus` and `ReservationStatusDate` directly encode the cancellation outcome — including them would constitute data leakage. `Company` is missing for 94.7% of bookings and carries no usable signal.

## Seasonal Demand Patterns

```{r eda-temporal, fig.cap = "Figure EDA-1: Monthly booking volume across 2015–2017.", fig.height = 4}
hotel_data %>%
  mutate(
    ArrivalDateMonth = factor(ArrivalDateMonth, levels = month.name),
    Year = factor(ArrivalDateYear)
  ) %>%
  count(ArrivalDateMonth, Year) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ArrivalDateMonth, y = n, colour = Year, group = Year)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("2015" = "#2166ac",
                                  "2016" = "#4dac26",
                                  "2017" = "#d01c8b")) +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 45)) +
  labs(title = "Monthly Booking Volume by Year",
       subtitle = "Consistent seasonal pattern across all three years",
       x = NULL, y = "Number of Bookings", colour = "Year") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

August dominates demand in every year while January and December are the quietest months. The seasonal rhythm is stable across 2015–2017 — not an artefact of one anomalous year. This stability has two modelling implications: arrival season is a reliable and meaningful predictor for all six models, and any model that ignores seasonality will systematically underperform.

## Distributions of Core Variables

```{r eda-distributions, fig.cap = "Figure EDA-2: Distributions of the four core numeric variables.", fig.height = 5}
p1 <- ggplot(hotel_data %>% filter(ADR > 0, ADR < 500), aes(x = ADR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(hotel_data$ADR[hotel_data$ADR > 0]),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "darkred", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(prefix = "€")) +
  labs(title = "Room Price (ADR)", x = "€/night", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

p2 <- ggplot(hotel_data, aes(x = LeadTime)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "darkorange", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(hotel_data$LeadTime),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "darkred", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Lead Time", x = "Days before arrival", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

p3 <- hotel_data %>%
  filter(total_stays > 0, total_stays <= 12) %>%
  count(total_stays) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = total_stays, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "seagreen", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  labs(title = "Total Nights Booked", x = "Nights", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

p4 <- hotel_data %>%
  count(TotalOfSpecialRequests) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = TotalOfSpecialRequests, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "mediumpurple", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:5) +
  labs(title = "Special Requests", x = "Number of requests", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

(p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4)
```

ADR and lead time are both strongly right-skewed with long upper tails — this has direct modelling consequences. ADR must be log-transformed before serving as a response variable in the Linear Model; lead time's skew means a small number of bookings made 300–500 days in advance would exert disproportionate leverage on any linear fit. Both are centred before modelling so intercepts represent realistic baseline profiles. Stay length and special requests are discrete counts concentrated at low values, consistent with a Poisson distribution, confirming that count-regression methods are appropriate.

## Market Segment as the Primary Organising Variable

```{r eda-segment-overview, fig.cap = "Figure EDA-3: Mean ADR, mean stay length, and cancellation rate by market segment.", fig.height = 4}
seg_summary <- hotel_data %>%
  filter(!as.character(MarketSegment) %in% c("Undefined")) %>%
  group_by(MarketSegment) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_adr    = mean(ADR[ADR > 0], na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_stays  = mean(total_stays[total_stays > 0], na.rm = TRUE),
    cancel_rate = mean(IsCanceled),
    n           = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

p_adr_seg <- ggplot(seg_summary,
                    aes(x = reorder(as.character(MarketSegment), mean_adr),
                        y = mean_adr,
                        fill = as.character(MarketSegment))) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("€", round(mean_adr))), hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 145)) +
  labs(title = "Mean ADR", x = NULL, y = "€/night") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

p_stays_seg <- ggplot(seg_summary,
                      aes(x = reorder(as.character(MarketSegment), mean_adr),
                          y = mean_stays,
                          fill = as.character(MarketSegment))) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_stays, 1)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 5)) +
  labs(title = "Mean Stay", x = NULL, y = "Nights") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

p_cancel_seg <- ggplot(seg_summary,
                       aes(x = reorder(as.character(MarketSegment), mean_adr),
                           y = cancel_rate,
                           fill = as.character(MarketSegment))) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(cancel_rate, accuracy = 0.1)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), limits = c(0, 0.95)) +
  labs(title = "Cancellation Rate", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

p_adr_seg + p_stays_seg + p_cancel_seg
```

Market segment simultaneously separates bookings by price, stay length, and cancellation risk — the three dimensions of this entire report. Direct bookings command the highest mean ADR (€122), reflecting that guests who book directly accept fewer intermediary discounts and tend to be more purposeful travellers. Groups sit at the opposite end on cancellation rate (69%), consistent with group bookings being tentative and subject to headcount changes. Online TA dominates volume at 48.9% of all bookings, making it the single most consequential segment for any revenue decision. Corporate guests stay the shortest, confirming that business travel generates revenue through price rather than nights.

## Two Data Quality Issues That Require Action

```{r eda-quality, fig.cap = "Figure EDA-4: Cancellation rate by deposit type (left) and ADR distribution highlighting the zero-price cluster (right).", fig.height = 4}
p_dep <- hotel_data %>%
  group_by(DepositType) %>%
  summarise(rate = mean(IsCanceled), n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(DepositType, rate), y = rate, fill = DepositType)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(scales::percent(rate, accuracy = 0.1),
                               "\n(n=", scales::comma(n), ")")),
            hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No Deposit"  = "steelblue",
                               "Non Refund"  = "tomato",
                               "Refundable"  = "darkorange")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1.2)) +
  labs(title = "Cancellation Rate by Deposit Type",
       subtitle = "Non Refund = 99.8% — likely a recording artefact",
       x = NULL, y = "Cancellation Rate") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

p_zero_adr <- hotel_data %>%
  mutate(zero_adr = ifelse(ADR == 0, "Zero ADR\n(complimentary)", "ADR > 0")) %>%
  filter(ADR < 500) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ADR, fill = zero_adr)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 70, colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Zero ADR\n(complimentary)" = "tomato",
                               "ADR > 0" = "steelblue"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(prefix = "€")) +
  labs(title = "ADR Distribution",
       subtitle = "1,208 zero-ADR bookings excluded from pricing model",
       x = "ADR (€/night)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

p_dep + p_zero_adr
```

Two findings here require explicit handling before any model is fitted. The 99.8% cancellation rate for Non Refund bookings is not a genuine behavioural signal — no hotel segment cancels at near certainty. The most credible explanation is a back-office recording convention where no-shows and agent-initiated failures are logged as "cancelled" regardless of payment status. This variable is included in all cancellation models because it genuinely separates booking populations and improves prediction, but its coefficient cannot be interpreted causally and should not be treated as a business lever.

The 1,208 zero-ADR bookings represent complimentary rooms — gifted stays not priced by the market. Including them would corrupt any model of room price by pulling the mean downward. They are excluded from Model 1 but retained in Models 3–6 where ADR is a predictor rather than the outcome.

## The Nonlinear Lead Time — Cancellation Relationship

```{r eda-leadtime, fig.cap = "Figure EDA-5: Estimated cancellation probability as a function of lead time (LOESS smoother, n = 10,000 random subsample).", fig.height = 4}
set.seed(2026)
hotel_data %>%
  slice_sample(n = 10000) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = LeadTime, y = IsCanceled)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.35,
              colour = "steelblue", fill = "lightblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(hotel_data$IsCanceled),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "darkred", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 420, y = mean(hotel_data$IsCanceled) + 0.03,
           label = paste0("Overall rate = ",
                          scales::percent(mean(hotel_data$IsCanceled), accuracy = 0.1)),
           colour = "darkred", size = 3.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 500)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), limits = c(0, 0.85)) +
  labs(title = "Cancellation Probability by Lead Time",
       subtitle = "LOESS smoother — risk rises steeply, then plateaus after ~150 days",
       x = "Lead Time (days before arrival)",
       y = "Estimated Cancellation Probability") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

This is the single most consequential plot in the EDA. Cancellation risk rises steeply for bookings made up to approximately 150 days in advance — then clearly plateaus. A guest booking 300 days out is not meaningfully riskier than one booking 200 days out. This plateau likely reflects committed long-horizon planners: conference attendees, anniversary travellers, families coordinating around school calendars who book early by necessity, not indecision. A model that imposes a straight line through this curve — as the Binomial GLM must — will overestimate risk for this group and potentially underestimate it at the steepest part of the early rise. This single observation is the primary technical motivation for the GAM in Model 4.

## What the EDA Tells Us Before Any Model Is Fitted

Five decisions follow directly from this section and are applied consistently across all six models:

1. **Log-transform ADR** for the Linear Model — the right skew violates normality and would distort coefficient estimates.
2. **Exclude zero-ADR records** from pricing models — complimentary rooms are not market prices.
3. **Exclude zero-night stays** from the Poisson model — 331 bookings with no recorded stay cannot be meaningfully modelled as a count outcome.
4. **Centre continuous predictors** (lead time, temperature) so that model intercepts represent realistic baseline profiles rather than impossible values of zero days and zero degrees.
5. **Flag Non Refund deposit** in all cancellation models — include for prediction accuracy, never interpret causally.

# Model 1: Linear Model — What Drives Room Price?

*Section lead: Divya Shori*

## Research Question

> **Which booking and seasonal characteristics determine the average daily rate a guest pays, and by how much?**

Room price is the primary revenue lever in a hotel. Even small systematic differences across segments or seasons compound across thousands of bookings into significant revenue outcomes. This model builds the evidential basis for differential pricing: not a heuristic but a quantified, controlled estimate — "Direct bookings sustain a 12% price premium over Online TA, holding season, room type, and lead time constant."

## Why a Linear Model?

ADR is a continuous, positive amount. Once log-transformed to address right skew, it behaves approximately as a Gaussian variable on the linear scale, making the Linear Model the natural and principled choice. The log transformation carries a further advantage: coefficients become multiplicative percentage effects on price, which is the language revenue managers use. A coefficient of 0.10 means a 10% price premium. No other model class produces this combination of interpretability and correctness for a log-normal response.

## Data Preparation and Motivation for log(ADR)

```{r lm-motivation-plot, fig.cap = "Figure 1: Raw ADR (left) is strongly right-skewed. After log-transformation (right) the distribution is approximately symmetric — confirming that log(ADR) is the correct response variable.", fig.height = 4}
hotel_lm <- hotel_data %>%
  filter(ADR > 0,
         !as.character(MarketSegment) %in% c("Complementary", "Undefined")) %>%
  mutate(
    log_adr      = log(ADR),
    LeadTime_c   = LeadTime   - mean(LeadTime,   na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_temp_c_c = avg_temp_c - mean(avg_temp_c, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
hotel_lm$MarketSegment <- droplevels(hotel_lm$MarketSegment)

p_raw <- ggplot(hotel_lm, aes(x = ADR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 80, fill = "tomato", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(prefix = "€"), limits = c(0, 600)) +
  labs(title = "Raw ADR", subtitle = "Right-skewed — violates LM normality assumption",
       x = "ADR (€/night)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p_log <- ggplot(hotel_lm, aes(x = log_adr)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(hotel_lm$log_adr),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(hotel_lm$log_adr) + 0.15, y = Inf, vjust = 2,
           label = paste0("Mean = €", round(exp(mean(hotel_lm$log_adr)), 1)), size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "log(ADR)", subtitle = "Approximately symmetric — suitable for LM",
       x = "log(ADR)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p_raw + p_log
```

The transformation is not cosmetic — it is a prerequisite for a valid Linear Model. On the log scale, every coefficient is a multiplicative percentage effect on price, directly comparable to how revenue managers think about pricing premiums. Two continuous predictors are mean-centred before fitting: lead time (mean = `r mean_lt` days) and monthly temperature (mean = `r mean_temp`°C). Centring ensures the model intercept has a concrete interpretation — the expected room price for the most common booking profile at average lead time and average temperature — rather than an extrapolation to impossible values.

`Online TA` is set as the reference level for market segment (49% of bookings) and `Transient` for customer type (75% of bookings), ensuring the intercept represents the most common booking profile.

## Exploring Key Predictors

```{r lm-eda, fig.cap = "Figure 2: log(ADR) by market segment (left) and by lead time (right).", fig.height = 4}
p_seg <- ggplot(hotel_lm,
                aes(x = reorder(MarketSegment, log_adr, median),
                    y = log_adr, fill = MarketSegment)) +
  geom_violin(trim = TRUE, alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, fill = "white", outlier.shape = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0("€", round(exp(x))),
                     sec.axis = sec_axis(~ ., name = "log(ADR)")) +
  labs(title = "Room Price by Market Segment", x = NULL, y = "ADR (€) [log scale]") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

p_lead <- ggplot(hotel_lm %>% sample_n(8000), aes(x = LeadTime, y = log_adr)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12, size = 0.7, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.4,
              colour = "darkred", fill = "salmon", linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 400)) +
  labs(title = "Lead Time vs. Room Price",
       x = "Lead Time (days before arrival)", y = "log(ADR)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

p_seg + p_lead
```

Market segment is a strong price discriminator — Direct bookings sit clearly above Groups and Corporate. The lead time scatter shows a modest but consistent negative association: bookings made further in advance tend to achieve lower prices, consistent with early-bird discount strategies. Crucially, the LOESS smoother is approximately linear here — unlike the cancellation relationship in Figure EDA-5 — which justifies the Linear Model's treatment of lead time as a linear predictor for this response variable.

## Model Fitting

```{r lm-split, cache = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
idx_lm   <- createDataPartition(hotel_lm$log_adr, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train_lm <- hotel_lm[idx_lm, ]
test_lm  <- hotel_lm[-idx_lm, ]
cat("Training:", nrow(train_lm), "| Test:", nrow(test_lm), "\n")
```

```{r lm-fit, cache = TRUE, dependson = "lm-split"}
model_lm <- lm(
  log_adr ~ arrival_season + MarketSegment + CustomerType +
            ReservedRoomType + LeadTime_c + TotalOfSpecialRequests +
            IsRepeatedGuest + Meal + is_via_agent + avg_temp_c_c,
  data = train_lm
)

cat(sprintf("Adjusted R²  : %.3f\n", summary(model_lm)$adj.r.squared))
cat(sprintf("Residual SE  : %.3f log-ADR units\n", summary(model_lm)$sigma))
```

## Formal Predictor Testing with drop1()

Rather than relying on individual coefficient p-values — which are unreliable for multi-level factors where no single coefficient captures the full effect — we apply `drop1()` with an F-test to assess the contribution of each predictor to the overall model.

```{r lm-drop1, dependson = "lm-fit", fig.cap = "Figure 3: F-statistics from drop1() for each predictor. The dashed line marks the critical F-value at α = 0.05.", fig.height = 5}
drop1_res <- drop1(model_lm, test = "F")

drop1_df <- as.data.frame(drop1_res) %>%
  rownames_to_column("Predictor") %>%
  filter(Predictor != "<none>") %>%
  mutate(Predictor = dplyr::recode(Predictor,
    "arrival_season"         = "Arrival Season",
    "MarketSegment"          = "Market Segment",
    "CustomerType"           = "Customer Type",
    "ReservedRoomType"       = "Reserved Room Type",
    "LeadTime_c"             = "Lead Time (centred)",
    "TotalOfSpecialRequests" = "Special Requests",
    "IsRepeatedGuest"        = "Repeated Guest",
    "Meal"                   = "Meal Plan",
    "is_via_agent"           = "Booked via Agent",
    "avg_temp_c_c"           = "Avg Temperature (centred)"
  ))

crit_f <- qf(0.95, df1 = 1, df2 = df.residual(model_lm))

ggplot(drop1_df, aes(x = `F value`, y = reorder(Predictor, `F value`))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = `F value`, yend = reorder(Predictor, `F value`)),
               colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = `Pr(>F)` < 0.05), size = 4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "steelblue", "FALSE" = "grey50"),
                      labels = c("TRUE" = "Significant (p < 0.05)", "FALSE" = "Not significant"),
                      name = NULL) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = crit_f, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "darkred", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = crit_f + 5, y = 1,
           label = paste0("Critical F = ", round(crit_f, 1)),
           colour = "darkred", size = 3.2, hjust = 0) +
  labs(title = "Predictor Importance: drop1() F-Statistics",
       subtitle = "Each bar shows how much model fit deteriorates when that predictor is removed",
       x = "F-statistic", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Every predictor in the model clears the significance threshold — the model contains no dead weight. The ranking is directly informative: room type and market segment generate the largest F-statistics, confirming that price is primarily a function of what was booked and through which channel. Arrival season and meal plan follow closely, reflecting peak-demand premiums and the added value of inclusive packages. Lead time and temperature sit lower but remain significant — their effects are real, just smaller in magnitude relative to the dominant structural drivers.

## The Pure Effect of Lead Time: Added-Variable Plot

A simple scatter of log(ADR) against lead time conflates the lead time effect with everything else that varies with it — segments that tend to book far in advance, seasons with different pricing, and so on. An added-variable plot removes this confounding by showing only what lead time explains *after* every other predictor has already been accounted for.

```{r lm-avplot, dependson = "lm-fit", fig.cap = "Figure 4: Added-variable plot for lead time. Both axes are residuals after removing all other predictors. The negative slope is the pure, unconfounded effect of lead time on room price.", fig.height = 4}
model_no_lt <- lm(
  log_adr ~ arrival_season + MarketSegment + CustomerType +
            ReservedRoomType + TotalOfSpecialRequests +
            IsRepeatedGuest + Meal + is_via_agent + avg_temp_c_c,
  data = train_lm
)
model_lt_on_x <- lm(
  LeadTime_c ~ arrival_season + MarketSegment + CustomerType +
               ReservedRoomType + TotalOfSpecialRequests +
               IsRepeatedGuest + Meal + is_via_agent + avg_temp_c_c,
  data = train_lm
)

av_df <- data.frame(
  resid_y  = residuals(model_no_lt),
  resid_lt = residuals(model_lt_on_x)
)

ggplot(av_df %>% sample_n(6000), aes(x = resid_lt, y = resid_y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12, size = 0.7, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "darkred", fill = "salmon",
              linewidth = 1.2, se = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Added-Variable Plot: Lead Time → Room Price",
       subtitle = "Pure effect of lead time after controlling for all other predictors",
       x = "Lead Time residuals (days — unexplained by other predictors)",
       y = "log(ADR) residuals (unexplained by other predictors)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

The negative slope is unambiguous and is not an artefact of confounding with season or market segment. After removing the influence of every other predictor in the model, guests who book earlier still pay less. The practical implication is direct: early-booking discounts are not simply a consequence of different guest profiles — they reflect a genuine pricing dynamic where advance purchase is rewarded, and the hotel can justify structured early-bird pricing tiers on this evidence.

## Marginal Effect: What Does a 200-Day Booking Cost?

```{r lm-marginal, dependson = "lm-fit", fig.cap = "Figure 5: Predicted ADR as a function of lead time for a typical reference booking. Shaded band = 95% confidence interval.", fig.height = 4}
lead_seq    <- seq(0, 400, by = 2)
mean_lt_val <- mean(train_lm$LeadTime, na.rm = TRUE)
mode_room   <- names(sort(table(train_lm$ReservedRoomType), decreasing = TRUE))[1]

newdata_lt <- data.frame(
  LeadTime_c             = lead_seq - mean_lt_val,
  MarketSegment          = factor("Online TA",  levels = levels(train_lm$MarketSegment)),
  CustomerType           = factor("Transient",  levels = levels(train_lm$CustomerType)),
  arrival_season         = factor("Summer",     levels = levels(train_lm$arrival_season)),
  ReservedRoomType       = factor(mode_room,    levels = levels(train_lm$ReservedRoomType)),
  Meal                   = factor("BB",         levels = levels(train_lm$Meal)),
  TotalOfSpecialRequests = mean(train_lm$TotalOfSpecialRequests, na.rm = TRUE),
  IsRepeatedGuest        = 0L,
  is_via_agent           = 1L,
  avg_temp_c_c           = 0
)

preds_lt       <- predict(model_lm, newdata = newdata_lt, interval = "confidence")
newdata_lt$fit <- exp(preds_lt[, "fit"])
newdata_lt$lwr <- exp(preds_lt[, "lwr"])
newdata_lt$upr <- exp(preds_lt[, "upr"])

ggplot(newdata_lt, aes(x = lead_seq)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean_lt_val, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = mean_lt_val + 8, y = max(newdata_lt$upr) * 0.98,
           label = paste0("Mean lead time\n(", round(mean_lt_val), " days)"),
           size = 3.2, colour = "grey40", hjust = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format(prefix = "€")) +
  labs(title = "Marginal Effect of Lead Time on Room Price",
       subtitle = "Reference: Online TA · Transient · Summer · BB meal · via agent",
       x = "Lead Time (days before arrival)",
       y = "Predicted ADR (€/night)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

For the reference booking profile, the model predicts a price decline of roughly €20–25 across the full range from last-minute to 400 days ahead. A guest booking tomorrow pays around €20 more per night than one who booked six months ago — a meaningful difference at scale but not a dramatic one. Last-minute rates can be set at a modest premium without triggering significant demand loss, while early-bird discounts of 10–15% are consistent with the data.

## Model Diagnostics

```{r lm-diagnostics, dependson = "lm-fit", fig.cap = "Figure 6: Residual diagnostics. Broadly homoscedastic spread and approximate normality confirm the log-transformation was appropriate.", fig.height = 4}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
plot(model_lm, which = 1, main = "Residuals vs Fitted",
     col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.3), pch = 16, cex = 0.5)
plot(model_lm, which = 2, main = "Normal Q-Q",
     col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.5), pch = 16, cex = 0.5)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The residuals vs. fitted plot shows no strong systematic pattern — variance is broadly stable across the fitted range. The Q-Q plot confirms approximate normality through the central range, with modest tail deviations typical for datasets of this size. These diagnostics confirm that the log-transformation successfully addressed the skewness identified in Figure 1.

## Out-of-Sample Performance

```{r lm-test, dependson = "lm-fit"}
pred_lm  <- predict(model_lm, newdata = test_lm)
rmse_lm  <- sqrt(mean((pred_lm - test_lm$log_adr)^2))
r2_test  <- cor(pred_lm, test_lm$log_adr)^2
rmse_eur <- exp(mean(test_lm$log_adr) + rmse_lm) - exp(mean(test_lm$log_adr))

cat(sprintf("Adjusted R² (train): %.3f\n", summary(model_lm)$adj.r.squared))
cat(sprintf("R² on test set:      %.3f\n", r2_test))
cat(sprintf("Approx. error in €:  ±€%.1f per night\n", abs(rmse_eur)))
```

```{r lm-pred-vs-actual, dependson = "lm-test", fig.cap = "Figure 7: Predicted vs. observed ADR on the held-out test set. Points cluster tightly around the 45° perfect-prediction line.", fig.height = 4}
data.frame(predicted = pred_lm, observed = test_lm$log_adr) %>%
  sample_n(3000) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = exp(predicted), y = exp(observed))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
              colour = "darkred", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(prefix = "€"), limits = c(0, 600)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format(prefix = "€"), limits = c(0, 600)) +
  labs(title = "Predicted vs. Observed ADR — Test Set",
       subtitle = "Red dashed line = perfect prediction",
       x = "Predicted ADR (€/night)", y = "Observed ADR (€/night)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

## Business Takeaway

The Linear Model explains `r round(summary(model_lm)$adj.r.squared * 100, 1)`% of room price variance on the training set, with an out-of-sample R² of `r round(r2_test, 3)` and a practical prediction error of approximately ±€`r round(abs(rmse_eur), 1)` per night — confirming genuine out-of-sample generalisation without overfitting. Three findings translate directly into commercial decisions. First, market segment is the dominant price driver: Direct bookings sustain the highest rates, which justifies investing in direct channel marketing to shift the booking mix toward higher-margin customers. Second, Summer arrivals attract a meaningful seasonal premium; off-peak rate strategies should account for this baseline. Third, the negative lead-time effect provides a data-grounded argument for structured early-bird pricing tiers that reward advance commitment while protecting last-minute rate integrity.

# Model 2: Poisson GLM — Who Stays Longest?

*Section lead: Divya Shori*

## Research Question

> **Which guest segments and booking characteristics predict longer stays, and how large are the differences across segments?**

A guest who stays four nights generates roughly twice the revenue of a two-night guest, with proportionally lower per-night operational cost. Yet most channel and marketing strategies are optimised for price or cancellation rate, not stay length. This model quantifies which segments stay longest — and by how much — providing the evidential basis for targeted long-stay promotions.

## Why a Poisson GLM?

`total_stays` is a non-negative integer count. A Linear Model is inappropriate — it can predict negative values and treats fractional nights as equally plausible. The Poisson GLM models the log of the expected count as a linear function of predictors, guarantees non-negative predictions, and produces **rate ratios** directly interpretable as "segment X stays Y% longer than the reference." Before accepting the Poisson assumption, we formally test for overdispersion — the common real-world violation where variance exceeds the mean, causing Poisson standard errors to be underestimated and inference to be anti-conservative.

## Data Preparation

```{r poisson-dist, fig.cap = "Figure 8: Observed stay length (blue) vs. the theoretical Poisson distribution at the observed mean (red).", fig.height = 4}
hotel_pois <- hotel_data %>%
  filter(total_stays > 0,
         !as.character(MarketSegment) %in% c("Undefined"))
hotel_pois$MarketSegment <- droplevels(hotel_pois$MarketSegment)

obs_lambda  <- mean(hotel_pois$total_stays)
max_display <- 14

pois_theoretical <- data.frame(
  nights   = 1:max_display,
  expected = dpois(1:max_display, lambda = obs_lambda) * nrow(hotel_pois)
)

hotel_pois %>%
  filter(total_stays <= max_display) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = total_stays)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(count)), binwidth = 1,
                 fill = "steelblue", colour = "white", alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(data = pois_theoretical, aes(x = nights, y = expected),
            colour = "darkred", linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = pois_theoretical, aes(x = nights, y = expected),
             colour = "darkred", size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:max_display) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Total Nights Booked",
       subtitle = paste0("Observed (blue) vs. Poisson(λ = ", round(obs_lambda, 2), ") (red)"),
       x = "Total Nights Booked", y = "Number of Bookings") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

The theoretical Poisson curve fits reasonably at low counts but falls well short of the observed frequencies at 4–8 nights. The data's right tail is heavier than a Poisson distribution predicts — a visual indicator that variance exceeds the mean. We confirm this formally below.

```{r poisson-meanvar, fig.cap = "Figure 9: Mean vs. variance of total nights across market segment × season groups. Points above the Var = Mean line confirm systematic overdispersion.", fig.height = 4}
mv_data <- hotel_pois %>%
  group_by(MarketSegment, arrival_season) %>%
  summarise(
    group_mean = mean(total_stays),
    group_var  = var(total_stays),
    n          = n(),
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(n >= 30)

ggplot(mv_data, aes(x = group_mean, y = group_var,
                    colour = MarketSegment, size = n)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
              colour = "darkred", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.3, y = 1.2,
           label = "Var = Mean\n(Poisson assumption)", colour = "darkred",
           size = 3.2, hjust = 0) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 9), name = "Bookings in group") +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Market Segment") +
  labs(title = "Mean–Variance Relationship by Segment and Season",
       subtitle = "Points above the dashed line signal overdispersion (Var > Mean)",
       x = "Group Mean (nights)", y = "Group Variance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

Nearly every segment–season combination sits above the Var = Mean line. Overdispersion is not confined to one unusual subgroup — it is a structural feature of this data. Standard Poisson standard errors would be too narrow, leading to over-rejection of null hypotheses. The quasi-Poisson correction below addresses this by scaling standard errors upward while leaving coefficients unchanged.

## Model Fitting and Overdispersion Correction

```{r poisson-fit, cache = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
idx_pois   <- createDataPartition(hotel_pois$total_stays, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train_pois <- hotel_pois[idx_pois, ]
test_pois  <- hotel_pois[-idx_pois, ]

model_pois <- glm(
  total_stays ~ MarketSegment + CustomerType + arrival_season +
                DepositType + IsRepeatedGuest + Meal +
                avg_temp_c + precipitation_mm + country_region,
  data = train_pois, family = poisson
)

disp_ratio <- deviance(model_pois) / df.residual(model_pois)
cat(sprintf("Dispersion ratio (Deviance / df): %.2f\n", disp_ratio))
cat(sprintf("→ %s\n",
    ifelse(disp_ratio > 1.5,
           "Overdispersion confirmed — refitting with quasi-Poisson.",
           "No strong overdispersion — Poisson retained.")))
```

```{r quasipoisson-refit, cache = TRUE, dependson = "poisson-fit"}
if (disp_ratio > 1.5) {
  model_pois <- glm(
    total_stays ~ MarketSegment + CustomerType + arrival_season +
                  DepositType + IsRepeatedGuest + Meal +
                  avg_temp_c + precipitation_mm + country_region,
    data = train_pois, family = quasipoisson
  )
  cat("Quasi-Poisson fitted. Coefficients unchanged; SEs corrected upward.\n")
}

model_null <- glm(total_stays ~ 1, data = train_pois, family = quasipoisson)
anova(model_null, model_pois, test = "F")
```

The dispersion ratio of `r round(disp_ratio, 2)` confirms severe overdispersion. The quasi-Poisson model corrects this by scaling standard errors upward by √`r round(disp_ratio, 2)` ≈ `r round(sqrt(disp_ratio), 2)`. Critically, the coefficients (rate ratios) are identical to standard Poisson — only the uncertainty estimates change, and they change in the direction of honesty. The F-test against the null model confirms that the predictors collectively explain significant variation in stay length.

## Rate Ratio Forest Plot

```{r poisson-forest, dependson = "quasipoisson-refit", fig.cap = "Figure 10: Rate ratios from the quasi-Poisson GLM with 95% confidence intervals. Values above 1× indicate longer expected stays than the reference group.", fig.height = 7}
pois_tidy <- tidy(model_pois, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    rr      = exp(estimate),
    rr_low  = exp(conf.low),
    rr_high = exp(conf.high)
  ) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
    significant = p.value < 0.05,
    term_clean  = term %>%
      str_replace("MarketSegment",    "Segment: ") %>%
      str_replace("CustomerType",     "Customer: ") %>%
      str_replace("arrival_season",   "Season: ") %>%
      str_replace("DepositType",      "Deposit: ") %>%
      str_replace("country_region",   "Region: ") %>%
      str_replace("Meal",             "Meal: ") %>%
      str_replace("avg_temp_c",       "Avg Temperature") %>%
      str_replace("precipitation_mm", "Precipitation") %>%
      str_replace("IsRepeatedGuest",  "Repeated Guest")
  ) %>%
  arrange(rr)

ggplot(pois_tidy, aes(x = rr, y = reorder(term_clean, rr), colour = significant)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = rr_low, xmax = rr_high), height = 0.35, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "steelblue", "FALSE" = "grey60"),
                      labels = c("TRUE" = "p < 0.05", "FALSE" = "p ≥ 0.05"),
                      name = "Significance") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0.4, 1.8, by = 0.2),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(x, "×")) +
  labs(title = "Rate Ratios: Quasi-Poisson GLM for Total Nights Booked",
       subtitle = "Values > 1× = longer stays than reference; < 1× = shorter",
       x = "Rate Ratio [exp(β)]", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Corporate customers show the lowest rate ratio — they stay the shortest of all customer types, consistent with single-night business trips. Guests on full-board and half-board meal plans stay significantly longer than BB guests: pre-committing to meals signals a structurally longer, holiday-oriented trip. Summer arrivals generate longer stays than all other seasons, driven by leisure travellers with more flexible schedules. Repeated guests stay longer than first-time visitors, likely because familiarity reduces friction and increases the perceived value of extending a stay.

## Post-Hoc Contrasts: Which Segments Differ?

```{r poisson-glht, dependson = "quasipoisson-refit", fig.cap = "Figure 11: Tukey-corrected pairwise contrasts between market segments.", fig.height = 6}
glht_pois <- glht(model_pois, linfct = mcp(MarketSegment = "Tukey"))

glht_df <- as.data.frame(confint(glht_pois)$confint) %>%
  rownames_to_column("Contrast") %>%
  rename(estimate = Estimate, lower = lwr, upper = upr) %>%
  mutate(
    rr          = exp(estimate),
    rr_low      = exp(lower),
    rr_high     = exp(upper),
    significant = !(rr_low <= 1 & rr_high >= 1)
  )

ggplot(glht_df, aes(x = rr, y = reorder(Contrast, rr), colour = significant)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = rr_low, xmax = rr_high), height = 0.4, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "darkred", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "steelblue", "FALSE" = "grey60"),
                      labels = c("TRUE" = "Significant (Tukey)", "FALSE" = "Not significant"),
                      name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "×")) +
  labs(title = "Pairwise Market Segment Contrasts: Stay Length",
       subtitle = "Tukey-corrected; rate ratio > 1× means first segment stays longer",
       x = "Rate Ratio (exp[contrast])", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The most robust distinctions are between Corporate bookings and every leisure-oriented segment — this gap is large, precise, and survives the multiple-comparison correction. Differences between Online TA and Direct are smaller and more uncertain. For a revenue manager, the actionable finding is the Corporate vs. leisure gap: stay-extension offers directed at Online TA leisure guests in Summer have the strongest evidence base; targeting Corporate guests for the same promotion is unlikely to move the needle.

## Test Set Performance and Business Takeaway

```{r poisson-test-performance, dependson = "quasipoisson-refit"}
pred_pois <- predict(model_pois, newdata = test_pois, type = "response")
mae_pois  <- mean(abs(pred_pois - test_pois$total_stays))
rmse_pois <- sqrt(mean((pred_pois - test_pois$total_stays)^2))
cat(sprintf("Mean Absolute Error: %.2f nights\n", mae_pois))
cat(sprintf("RMSE:                %.2f nights\n", rmse_pois))
```

The quasi-Poisson model predicts stay length to within approximately `r round(mae_pois, 1)` nights on unseen data — useful precision for segment-level planning. A discounted third or fourth night offered at the point of booking for stays above seven days could materially shift average length-of-stay upward for Summer Online TA leisure bookings, generating incremental revenue with minimal additional operational cost.

# Model 3: Binomial GLM — Which Bookings Will Cancel?

*Section lead: Lorena Zovkic*

## The Business Problem

Every cancellation is a double loss: the room sits empty, and the revenue that could have been earned from another guest is gone. The earlier a high-risk booking can be identified — at the moment of reservation, before any room is allocated — the more options the hotel has: a retention communication, an adjusted overbooking allowance, a targeted offer. This model answers a precise operational question: given only the information available on day one, how likely is it that this guest will cancel?

## Why Logistic Regression?

`IsCanceled` takes exactly two values. The Binomial GLM models the log-odds of cancellation as a linear function of the predictors, guaranteeing that every prediction stays within the valid probability range [0, 1]. The coefficients it produces are odds ratios — a directly actionable quantity that tells a revenue manager not just whether a predictor matters, but by how much and in which direction. Only information available at the time of booking is used as predictors.

The model carries one important assumption: each predictor contributes additively and linearly to the log-odds of cancellation. For most categorical predictors this is entirely reasonable. For lead time, Figure EDA-5 already showed the true relationship may curve. The Binomial GLM is fitted here as a transparent, interpretable baseline; Model 4 directly tests where linearity breaks down.

## Data Preparation

```{r binomial-prep, cache = TRUE}
hotel_bin <- hotel_data %>%
  filter(!as.character(MarketSegment) %in% c("Undefined", "Complementary"))
hotel_bin$MarketSegment <- droplevels(hotel_bin$MarketSegment)

# Shared colour palette for all cancellation model plots (Models 3–6).
# Defined here once; used in every subsequent plot chunk.
clr <- c(
  primary   = "#2E5FA3",
  secondary = "#E05A2B",
  neutral   = "#6B7280",
  success   = "#1E7A34",
  warning_c = "#B45309"
)

set.seed(2026)
idx_bin   <- createDataPartition(hotel_bin$IsCanceled, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train_bin <- hotel_bin[idx_bin, ]
test_bin  <- hotel_bin[-idx_bin, ]

cat(sprintf(
  "Training: %d | Test: %d | Cancellation rate (train): %.1f%%\n",
  nrow(train_bin), nrow(test_bin),
  mean(train_bin$IsCanceled) * 100
))
```

The 80/20 split is stratified on `IsCanceled` to preserve the 41.7% cancellation rate in both sets. The same `train_bin` and `test_bin` objects are reused identically for Models 4, 5, and 6 — this is the foundation for a fair four-way comparison.

## Exploratory Analysis

```{r binomial-eda, fig.cap = "Figure 12: Cancellation rate by deposit type (left) and cancellation probability by lead time (right).", fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4}
p_dep <- train_bin %>%

p_dep + p_lead
```

The left panel confirms the deposit-type artefact described in the EDA. The right panel reproduces — now on the training set only — the nonlinear lead-time pattern from Figure EDA-5. Both findings were anticipated; they are included here to confirm that the training split preserved the patterns of the full dataset.

## Model Fitting

```{r binomial-fit, cache = TRUE, dependson = "binomial-prep"}
model_binomial <- glm(
  IsCanceled ~ LeadTime + DepositType + MarketSegment +
    PreviousCancellations + TotalOfSpecialRequests +
    IsRepeatedGuest + BookingChanges + DaysInWaitingList +
    CustomerType + is_via_agent + arrival_season +
    avg_temp_c + precipitation_mm,
  data   = train_bin,
  family = binomial
)

null_dev <- model_binomial$null.deviance
res_dev  <- deviance(model_binomial)
mcf_r2   <- round(1 - res_dev / null_dev, 3)

cat(sprintf("Null deviance:      %.0f\n", null_dev))
cat(sprintf("Residual deviance:  %.0f  (%.0f%% reduction)\n",
            res_dev, (1 - res_dev / null_dev) * 100))
cat(sprintf("McFadden pseudo-R²: %.3f\n", mcf_r2))
```

## Formal Predictor Testing with drop1()

```{r binomial-drop1, dependson = "binomial-fit", fig.cap = "Figure 13: Chi-square statistics from drop1(). Each bar quantifies how much model fit deteriorates when that predictor is removed entirely.", fig.height = 5}
drop1_bin <- drop1(model_binomial, test = "Chisq")

drop1_bin_df <- as.data.frame(drop1_bin) %>%
  rownames_to_column("Predictor") %>%
  filter(Predictor != "<none>") %>%
  mutate(Predictor = dplyr::recode(Predictor,
    "LeadTime"               = "Lead Time",
    "DepositType"            = "Deposit Type",
    "MarketSegment"          = "Market Segment",
    "PreviousCancellations"  = "Previous Cancellations",
    "TotalOfSpecialRequests" = "Special Requests",
    "IsRepeatedGuest"        = "Repeated Guest",
    "BookingChanges"         = "Booking Changes",
    "DaysInWaitingList"      = "Days on Waiting List",
    "CustomerType"           = "Customer Type",
    "is_via_agent"           = "Booked via Agent",
    "arrival_season"         = "Arrival Season",
    "avg_temp_c"             = "Avg. Temperature",
    "precipitation_mm"       = "Precipitation"
  ))

crit_chi <- qchisq(0.95, df = 1)

ggplot(drop1_bin_df, aes(x = LRT, y = reorder(Predictor, LRT))) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = LRT > crit_chi), width = 0.65, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(LRT > 1000, paste0(round(LRT / 1000, 1), "k"),
                               as.character(round(LRT, 0)))),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3.1, colour = clr["neutral"]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = crit_chi, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = clr["secondary"], linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = crit_chi + 40, y = 0.7,
           label = paste0("α = 0.05\n(χ² = ", round(crit_chi, 1), ")"),
           colour = clr["secondary"], size = 3, hjust = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = clr["primary"], "FALSE" = clr["neutral"])) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
  labs(title = "Predictor Contribution: drop1() Chi-square Test",
       subtitle = "All predictors contribute significantly — none are redundant",
       x = "Chi-square Statistic (LRT)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = clr["neutral"], size = 9))
```

Every predictor clears the significance threshold. Previous cancellations and deposit type cause the largest model deterioration when removed, confirming that booking history and payment commitment are the strongest cancellation signals. Weather variables (temperature, precipitation) contribute modestly but remain statistically justified — they add marginal signal beyond arrival season at the cost of two parameters.

## Coefficient Interpretation: Odds Ratios

```{r binomial-forest, dependson = "binomial-fit", fig.cap = "Figure 14: Odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals on a log scale. Values right of the dashed line increase cancellation odds; values left reduce them. Non Refund deposit is excluded — its OR approaches infinity and reflects a recording artefact.", fig.height = 7.5, fig.width = 9}
bin_tidy <- tidy(model_binomial, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)", !grepl("Non.Refund", term)) %>%
  mutate(
    significant = p.value < 0.05,
    direction   = ifelse(estimate > 1, "Increases risk", "Reduces risk"),
    term_clean  = term %>%
      str_replace("MarketSegment",         "Segment: ") %>%
      str_replace("CustomerType",          "Customer: ") %>%
      str_replace("DepositTypeRefundable", "Deposit: Refundable") %>%
      str_replace("arrival_season",        "Season: ") %>%
      str_replace("LeadTime",              "Lead Time (per day)") %>%
      str_replace("PreviousCancellations", "Previous Cancellations") %>%
      str_replace("TotalOfSpecialRequests","Special Requests") %>%
      str_replace("IsRepeatedGuest",       "Repeated Guest") %>%
      str_replace("BookingChanges",        "Booking Changes") %>%
      str_replace("DaysInWaitingList",     "Days on Waiting List") %>%
      str_replace("is_via_agent",          "Booked via Agent") %>%
      str_replace("avg_temp_c",            "Avg. Temperature") %>%
      str_replace("precipitation_mm",      "Precipitation")
  )

ggplot(bin_tidy, aes(x = estimate, y = reorder(term_clean, estimate))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = clr["neutral"], linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = conf.low, xend = conf.high,
                   yend = reorder(term_clean, estimate)),
               colour = "grey80", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = significant, shape = direction), size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = clr["primary"], "FALSE" = "grey55"),
                      labels = c("TRUE" = "p < 0.05", "FALSE" = "p ≥ 0.05"),
                      name = "Significance") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Increases risk" = 17, "Reduces risk" = 19),
                     name = "Direction") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "×"),
                breaks = c(0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5, 8)) +
  labs(title = "Binomial GLM — Odds Ratios for Cancellation",
       subtitle = "Non Refund deposit omitted (OR ≈ ∞ — recording artefact)",
       x = "Odds Ratio [exp(β)] — log scale", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = clr["neutral"], size = 9))
```

Five findings stand out for operational interpretation. **Lead time:** the per-day OR of `r round(exp(coef(model_binomial)["LeadTime"]), 4)` compounds to `r round(exp(coef(model_binomial)["LeadTime"] * 30), 2)`× per 30 days — a booking made six months ahead carries roughly `r round(exp(coef(model_binomial)["LeadTime"]*180)/exp(coef(model_binomial)["LeadTime"]*7),1)`× higher odds than one made a week out. **Special requests:** each additional request reduces cancellation odds by `r round((1 - exp(coef(model_binomial)["TotalOfSpecialRequests"]))*100, 0)`% — the strongest protective factor, reflecting psychological commitment to the trip. **Previous cancellations:** each prior cancellation multiplies current odds by `r round(exp(coef(model_binomial)["PreviousCancellations"]), 2)`× — booking history is highly predictive and already sits in the hotel's reservation system. **Booking changes:** counterintuitively, each modification *reduces* odds by `r round((1-exp(coef(model_binomial)["BookingChanges"]))*100,0)`% — a guest actively managing their booking plans to show up. **Repeated guests:** returning visitors are `r round((1-exp(coef(model_binomial)["IsRepeatedGuest"]))*100,0)`% less likely to cancel, reflecting established commitment to the property.

## Marginal Effect of Lead Time

```{r binomial-marginal, dependson = "binomial-fit", fig.cap = "Figure 15: Predicted cancellation probability by lead time for a typical reference booking. The perfectly straight line is a structural consequence of the GLM's linearity assumption — Model 4 tests whether this is accurate.", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5}
lead_seq_bin <- seq(0, 400, by = 2)

newdata_bin <- data.frame(
  LeadTime               = lead_seq_bin,
  DepositType            = factor("No Deposit", levels = levels(train_bin$DepositType)),
  MarketSegment          = factor("Online TA",  levels = levels(train_bin$MarketSegment)),
  PreviousCancellations  = 0,

  arrival_season         = factor("Summer",     levels = levels(train_bin$arrival_season)),

  precipitation_mm       = mean(train_bin$precipitation_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
)

preds_bin            <- predict(model_binomial, newdata = newdata_bin,
                                type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
newdata_bin$prob     <- plogis(preds_bin$fit)
newdata_bin$prob_lwr <- plogis(preds_bin$fit - 1.96 * preds_bin$se.fit)
newdata_bin$prob_upr <- plogis(preds_bin$fit + 1.96 * preds_bin$se.fit)

ggplot(newdata_bin, aes(x = LeadTime)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = prob_lwr, ymax = prob_upr),
              fill = clr["primary"], alpha = 0.15) +

  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(train_bin$IsCanceled),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = clr["secondary"], linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 300, y = mean(train_bin$IsCanceled) + 0.04,
           label = paste0("Overall cancellation rate: ",
                          scales::percent(mean(train_bin$IsCanceled), accuracy = 0.1)),
           colour = clr["secondary"], size = 3, fontface = "italic") +
  annotate("text", x = 355, y = 0.80,
           label = "The GLM assumes\na straight-line increase.\nModel 4 tests this.",
           colour = clr["neutral"], size = 3, fontface = "italic", hjust = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), limits = c(0, 0.95)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 400)) +

       subtitle = "Reference: Online TA · Transient · No Deposit · Summer · 1 special request",
       x = "Lead Time (days before arrival)", y = "Predicted Cancellation Probability") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = clr["neutral"], size = 9))
```

## Test Set Performance

roc_bin        <- roc(test_bin$IsCanceled, pred_probs_bin, quiet = TRUE)

  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +

```{r binomial-confmat, dependson = "binomial-roc"}
pred_class_bin <- factor(ifelse(pred_probs_bin > 0.5, 1, 0))
cm_bin <- caret::confusionMatrix(pred_class_bin, factor(test_bin$IsCanceled),
                                  positive = "1")

```

## Business Takeaway

An AUC of `r round(auc(roc_bin), 3)` on unseen data means the model correctly ranks a randomly drawn cancellation above a randomly drawn non-cancellation `r round(auc(roc_bin)*100, 1)`% of the time — well above the 50% baseline of random guessing. For a revenue manager, three findings translate directly into action: any booking combining a lead time above 100 days, zero special requests, and at least one prior cancellation falls into the highest-risk tier and should trigger proactive retention; the protective effect of special requests suggests prompting guests to submit room or meal preferences within 48 hours of booking; and the counterintuitive booking-changes finding suggests that making modifications easy rather than friction-heavy reduces overall cancellation risk.
