# Model 4: Generalised Additive Model — Do Effects Follow a Straight Line?

*Section lead: Lorena Zovkic*

## The Question This Model Answers

The Binomial GLM is transparent and actionable — but it forces every continuous predictor's relationship with cancellation to be a straight line on the log-odds scale. We know from Figure EDA-5 that lead time does not behave this way. The GAM keeps the logistic regression framework but replaces linear terms for selected continuous predictors with flexible smooth functions that let the data determine the shape. Three questions:

1. Are the nonlinear patterns in the EDA statistically real, or smoothing artefacts?
2. Does correcting for them improve out-of-sample prediction?
3. Where exactly does the Binomial GLM go wrong — and what are the operational consequences?

## Why a GAM?

The GAM occupies a deliberate position in the modelling ladder (Table 0). It is more flexible than the Binomial GLM (drops linearity for continuous terms) but more constrained than the SVM and Neural Network (retains additivity — each smooth still operates independently). This makes it interpretable: the smooth effect of lead time can be plotted directly and explained to a revenue manager. The complexity of each smooth is determined automatically by penalised regression (REML) — the model uses only as much flexibility as the data justifies. The effective degrees of freedom (EDF) summarises this: EDF = 1 means the smooth collapsed to a straight line (the GLM assumption was correct); EDF >> 1 means genuine nonlinearity was detected.

## Model Fitting

```{r gam-fit, cache = TRUE, dependson = "binomial-prep"}
library(mgcv)

model_gam <- gam(
  IsCanceled ~ s(LeadTime) + s(ADR) + s(DaysInWaitingList) +
    DepositType + MarketSegment + PreviousCancellations +
    TotalOfSpecialRequests + IsRepeatedGuest +
    CustomerType + arrival_season +
    avg_temp_c + precipitation_mm,
  data   = train_bin,
  family = binomial,
  method = "REML"
)

gam_summ <- summary(model_gam)

smooth_table <- as.data.frame(gam_summ$s.table) %>%
  rownames_to_column("Term") %>%
  mutate(
    Term = dplyr::recode(Term,
      "s(LeadTime)"          = "s(Lead Time)",
      "s(ADR)"               = "s(ADR — room price)",
      "s(DaysInWaitingList)" = "s(Days on Waiting List)"
    ),
    Verdict = case_when(
      edf < 1.5 ~ "Approximately linear — GLM assumption holds",
      edf < 3.0 ~ "Mildly nonlinear — GLM slightly misrepresents this",
      TRUE      ~ "Clearly nonlinear — GLM was meaningfully wrong here"
    )
  )

kable(smooth_table %>% dplyr::select(Term, edf, `p-value`, Verdict),
      digits = c(0, 2, 4, 0),
      col.names = c("Smooth Term", "EDF", "p-value", "Verdict"),
      caption = "Table 4-1: EDF for the three smooth terms. EDF = 1 is a straight line; higher values indicate genuine nonlinearity that the Binomial GLM cannot represent.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = TRUE, font_size = 11) %>%
  row_spec(which(smooth_table$edf > 2), bold = TRUE, background = "#EFF6FF")

cat(sprintf("\nDeviance explained: %.1f%%\n", gam_summ$dev.expl * 100))
cat(sprintf("AIC:                %.1f\n",    AIC(model_gam)))
```

## What Shape Does Each Relationship Take?

```{r gam-smooths, dependson = "gam-fit", fig.cap = "Figure 17: Estimated smooth effects from the GAM. Each panel isolates one predictor's contribution to the log-odds of cancellation after controlling for all others. The EDF in each title quantifies departure from linearity.", fig.width = 12, fig.height = 4.5}
edf_lead <- round(gam_summ$s.table["s(LeadTime)",          "edf"], 1)
edf_adr  <- round(gam_summ$s.table["s(ADR)",               "edf"], 1)
edf_wl   <- round(gam_summ$s.table["s(DaysInWaitingList)", "edf"], 1)

# Extract smooth effects safely via predict(type = "terms").
# This approach builds a grid that varies one predictor while holding all
# others at their training-set means / modal values, avoiding the fragility
# of directly referencing model$model[1, ].
make_smooth_df <- function(model, var_name, x_label, n = 300) {
  col_data <- model$model[[var_name]]
  x_seq    <- seq(quantile(col_data, 0.01, na.rm = TRUE),
                  quantile(col_data, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE),
                  length.out = n)

  # Build a reference row using training-set means / modal factor levels
  ref_row <- as.data.frame(lapply(model$model, function(col) {
    if (is.numeric(col)) mean(col, na.rm = TRUE)
    else if (is.factor(col)) levels(col)[which.max(tabulate(col))]
    else col[1]
  }))
  ref_row <- ref_row[rep(1, n), ]
  ref_row[[var_name]] <- x_seq

  pt <- predict(model, newdata = ref_row, type = "terms", se.fit = TRUE)
  col_idx <- which(grepl(paste0("(", var_name, ")"), colnames(pt$fit), fixed = TRUE))[1]
  data.frame(x = x_seq, fit = as.numeric(pt$fit[, col_idx]),
             se = as.numeric(pt$se.fit[, col_idx]), x_lab = x_label)
}

d_lead <- make_smooth_df(model_gam, "LeadTime", "Lead Time (days before arrival)")
d_adr  <- make_smooth_df(model_gam, "ADR",      "Average Daily Rate — ADR (€/night)")
d_wl   <- make_smooth_df(model_gam, "DaysInWaitingList", "Days on Waiting List")

plot_smooth <- function(d, title_str, edf_val) {
  ggplot(d, aes(x = x)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = fit - 1.96 * se, ymax = fit + 1.96 * se),
                fill = clr["primary"], alpha = 0.15) +
    geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = clr["primary"], linewidth = 1.3) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
               colour = clr["neutral"], linewidth = 0.7) +
    labs(title = paste0(title_str, "  (EDF = ", edf_val, ")"),
         x = unique(d$x_lab), y = "Partial effect (log-odds)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

plot_smooth(d_lead, "s(Lead Time)", edf_lead) +
plot_smooth(d_adr,  "s(ADR)",      edf_adr) +
plot_smooth(d_wl,   "s(Days on Waiting List)", edf_wl)
```

Three panels, three distinct findings. **s(Lead Time) — EDF = `r edf_lead`:** The smooth confirms and quantifies the EDA finding. Risk rises steeply to around 100–150 days then clearly flattens. The GLM's straight line assigns ever-increasing risk past the plateau and meaningfully misrepresents both committed long-planners (overscored) and the steepest early-rise zone (underscored). **s(ADR) — EDF = `r edf_adr`:** Room price has a non-monotone relationship the GLM cannot capture — mid-range priced rooms carry the highest cancellation risk, while very cheap and very expensive rooms show lower risk. Price-sensitive guests use what they paid for; luxury bookings accompany specific purposeful trips; mid-range rooms attract the widest mix of opportunistic bookers. **s(Days on Waiting List) — EDF = `r edf_wl`:** The GAM chose not to use its extra flexibility here — a straight line fits as well as a curve. This is a valuable null result: not every predictor needs a smooth, and the model correctly identifies where the GLM's linearity assumption holds.

## Does the Flexibility Improve Prediction?

```{r gam-comparison, dependson = c("gam-fit", "binomial-fit")}
aic_glm  <- AIC(model_binomial)
aic_gam  <- AIC(model_gam)
aic_diff <- round(aic_glm - aic_gam, 0)

cat(sprintf("AIC — Binomial GLM: %.1f\n", aic_glm))
cat(sprintf("AIC — GAM:          %.1f\n", aic_gam))
cat(sprintf("AIC improvement:    %.0f points\n", aic_diff))
```

```{r gam-roc, dependson = c("gam-fit", "binomial-roc"), fig.cap = "Figure 18: ROC curves for the Binomial GLM and GAM on the same held-out test set. The shaded rectangle marks the operating range (FPR 10–35%) most relevant for a hotel risk-scoring system.", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5}
gam_probs <- predict(model_gam, newdata = test_bin, type = "response")
roc_gam   <- roc(test_bin$IsCanceled, gam_probs, quiet = TRUE)

glm_lbl <- paste0("Binomial GLM  (AUC = ", round(auc(roc_bin), 3), ")")
gam_lbl <- paste0("GAM           (AUC = ", round(auc(roc_gam), 3), ")")

bind_rows(
  data.frame(fpr = 1 - roc_bin$specificities,
             tpr = roc_bin$sensitivities, Model = glm_lbl),
  data.frame(fpr = 1 - roc_gam$specificities,
             tpr = roc_gam$sensitivities, Model = gam_lbl)
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fpr, y = tpr, colour = Model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
              colour = "grey65", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.05, xmax = 0.35, ymin = 0.55, ymax = 1.0,
           fill = "grey96", colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.3) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.20, y = 0.61,
           label = "Operationally relevant\nregion for risk scoring",
           colour = clr["neutral"], size = 2.8, fontface = "italic") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(c(clr["primary"], clr["secondary"]),
                                        c(glm_lbl, gam_lbl))) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "ROC Comparison: Binomial GLM vs. GAM",
       subtitle = "Same predictors, same data — difference reflects smooth terms only",
       x = "False Positive Rate", y = "True Positive Rate", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = clr["neutral"], size = 9))
```

```{r gam-confmat, dependson = "gam-roc"}
pred_class_gam <- factor(ifelse(gam_probs > 0.5, 1, 0))
cm_gam <- caret::confusionMatrix(pred_class_gam, factor(test_bin$IsCanceled),
                                  positive = "1")
cm_gam
```

The GAM achieves an AUC of `r round(auc(roc_gam), 3)` versus `r round(auc(roc_bin), 3)` for the GLM — a gain of `r round(auc(roc_gam) - auc(roc_bin), 3)` points on unseen data. The AIC drops by `r aic_diff` points, confirming the improvement is genuine and not overfitting.

## Where Exactly Do GLM and GAM Disagree?

```{r gam-marginal, dependson = c("gam-fit", "binomial-fit"), fig.cap = "Figure 19: Predicted cancellation probability from the GAM (solid) and GLM (dashed) for the same reference booking. Annotations identify the two zones of meaningful operational disagreement.", fig.width = 8.5, fig.height = 4.5}
newdata_gam <- data.frame(
  LeadTime               = lead_seq_bin,
  ADR                    = median(train_bin$ADR[train_bin$ADR > 0], na.rm = TRUE),
  DaysInWaitingList      = 0,
  DepositType            = factor("No Deposit", levels = levels(train_bin$DepositType)),
  MarketSegment          = factor("Online TA",  levels = levels(train_bin$MarketSegment)),
  PreviousCancellations  = 0,
  TotalOfSpecialRequests = 1,
  IsRepeatedGuest        = 0L,
  CustomerType           = factor("Transient",  levels = levels(train_bin$CustomerType)),
  arrival_season         = factor("Summer",     levels = levels(train_bin$arrival_season)),
  avg_temp_c             = mean(train_bin$avg_temp_c,       na.rm = TRUE),
  precipitation_mm       = mean(train_bin$precipitation_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
)

gam_link   <- predict(model_gam, newdata = newdata_gam, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
gam_margin <- data.frame(LeadTime = lead_seq_bin,
                         prob     = plogis(gam_link$fit),
                         prob_lwr = plogis(gam_link$fit - 1.96 * gam_link$se.fit),
                         prob_upr = plogis(gam_link$fit + 1.96 * gam_link$se.fit))

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = gam_margin,
              aes(x = LeadTime, ymin = prob_lwr, ymax = prob_upr),
              fill = clr["secondary"], alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_line(data = gam_margin,
            aes(x = LeadTime, y = prob, colour = gam_lbl), linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(LeadTime = lead_seq_bin, prob = newdata_bin$prob),
            aes(x = LeadTime, y = prob, colour = glm_lbl),
            linewidth = 1.1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("segment", x = 150, xend = 150, y = 0.05, yend = 0.87,
           linetype = "dotted", colour = clr["neutral"], linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 154, y = 0.84,
           label = "GAM plateau\nbegins ~150 days",
           colour = clr["neutral"], size = 2.9, fontface = "italic", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("label", x = 265, y = 0.52,
           label = "GLM overestimates\nrisk in this zone",
           colour = clr["primary"], size = 2.9, fill = "white", label.size = 0.25) +
  annotate("label", x = 22, y = 0.27,
           label = "GLM underestimates\nrisk here",
           colour = clr["primary"], size = 2.9, fill = "white", label.size = 0.25) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(c(clr["secondary"], clr["primary"]),
                                        c(gam_lbl, glm_lbl))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 400)) +
  labs(title = "Where Do GLM and GAM Disagree?",
       subtitle = "Reference: Online TA · Transient · No Deposit · Summer · median ADR · 1 special request",
       x = "Lead Time (days before arrival)",
       y = "Predicted Cancellation Probability", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = clr["neutral"], size = 9))
```

## Business Takeaway

The GAM is strictly better than the Binomial GLM for cancellation prediction — higher AUC on held-out data, lower AIC, and a more accurate representation of how lead time and ADR actually relate to cancellation risk. It achieves this without sacrificing interpretability: each smooth is a curve that can be shown to a revenue manager. Two operational implications follow from the smooth terms: lead-time risk plateaus after 150 days (treat bookings beyond that threshold as equivalent risk, free up overbooking capacity), and mid-range ADR rooms carry disproportionate risk (consider targeted deposit requirements for this price band). For the scoring layer, the GAM is the right model. For explaining a flagged booking to a commercial stakeholder, the GLM's odds ratios remain the cleaner communication tool — the two models are complementary.

---

# Model 5: Support Vector Machine

*Section lead: Petronela Tabalae*

## Research Question

> **Can an SVM improve cancellation classification beyond the GLM and GAM, and does the gain come from the kernel's ability to represent feature interactions?**

Both the GLM and GAM are additive: each predictor's contribution is independent of all others. Yet booking risk may not decompose this way. A long lead time may be routine for a Corporate guest and alarming for a leisure Online TA guest; a non-refundable deposit may eliminate risk for one customer type and merely defer it for another. If interactions of this kind shape cancellation, only models capable of representing nonlinear joint decision boundaries can capture them. The SVM with an RBF kernel is the canonical tool for this — and comparing it to a linear-kernel SVM isolates exactly how much of any gain comes from interactions versus other differences in how SVMs are trained.

## Data Preparation and Subsampling Rationale

```{r svm-setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(kernlab)
library(PRROC)
library(parallel)

set.seed(2026)
sub_idx       <- createDataPartition(train_bin$IsCanceled,
                                     p = 5000 / nrow(train_bin), list = FALSE)
svm_train_sub <- train_bin[sub_idx, ]

cat(sprintf("Full training set: %d | SVM subsample: %d | Test set: %d\n",
            nrow(train_bin), nrow(svm_train_sub), nrow(test_bin)))
cat(sprintf("Cancellation rate — full: %.3f | subsample: %.3f | test: %.3f\n",
            mean(train_bin$IsCanceled), mean(svm_train_sub$IsCanceled),
            mean(test_bin$IsCanceled)))
```

Kernel SVM training complexity grows roughly as O(n²) — fitting on the full `r format(nrow(train_bin), big.mark=",")` training rows with cross-validation is computationally infeasible on standard hardware. We work on a stratified 5,000-row subsample that preserves the 41.7% cancellation rate exactly. This is documented standard practice for kernel SVMs at this data scale. Critically, **the test set evaluation uses the full held-out test set** — reported test performance is directly comparable to Models 3 and 4.

```{r svm-formula-and-matrix}
svm_formula <- IsCanceled ~ LeadTime + DepositType + MarketSegment +
  PreviousCancellations + TotalOfSpecialRequests + IsRepeatedGuest +
  BookingChanges + DaysInWaitingList + CustomerType + is_via_agent +
  arrival_season + avg_temp_c + precipitation_mm

make_xy <- function(df, scaler = NULL) {
  X <- model.matrix(svm_formula, data = df)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
  if (is.null(scaler)) {
    scaler <- list(center = colMeans(X), scale = apply(X, 2, sd))
    scaler$scale[scaler$scale == 0] <- 1
  }
  X <- scale(X, center = scaler$center, scale = scaler$scale)
  list(X = X,
       y = factor(df$IsCanceled, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Stay", "Cancel")),
       scaler = scaler)
}

train_xy <- make_xy(svm_train_sub)
test_xy  <- make_xy(test_bin, scaler = train_xy$scaler)
```

## Cross-Validation for Kernel and Hyperparameter Selection

```{r svm-cv-tuning, cache = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
folds <- createFolds(svm_train_sub$IsCanceled, k = 5, returnTrain = FALSE)

n_cores <- max(1, min(5, parallel::detectCores() - 1))
cl <- parallel::makeCluster(n_cores)
parallel::clusterEvalQ(cl, { library(kernlab); library(pROC) })
parallel::clusterExport(cl, c("train_xy"))

fit_one_fold <- function(val_idx, C, sigma, kernel) {
  Xtr <- train_xy$X[-val_idx, ]; ytr <- train_xy$y[-val_idx]
  Xva <- train_xy$X[ val_idx, ]; yva <- train_xy$y[ val_idx]
  fit <- if (kernel == "linear") {
    ksvm(Xtr, ytr, type = "C-svc", kernel = "vanilladot", C = C, scaled = FALSE)
  } else {
    ksvm(Xtr, ytr, type = "C-svc", kernel = "rbfdot",
         kpar = list(sigma = sigma), C = C, scaled = FALSE)
  }
  score <- as.numeric(predict(fit, Xva, type = "decision"))
  as.numeric(pROC::auc(yva, score, levels = c("Stay", "Cancel"),
                        direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))
}

cv_auc <- function(C, sigma = NULL, kernel) {
  mean(unlist(parallel::parLapply(cl, folds, fit_one_fold,
                                   C = C, sigma = sigma, kernel = kernel)))
}

linear_grid <- expand.grid(C = c(0.1, 1, 10))
linear_grid$cv_auc <- mapply(function(C) cv_auc(C, kernel = "linear"), linear_grid$C)

rbf_grid <- expand.grid(C = c(0.1, 1, 10), sigma = c(0.01, 0.1, 1))
rbf_grid$cv_auc <- mapply(function(C, s) cv_auc(C, sigma = s, kernel = "rbf"),
                           rbf_grid$C, rbf_grid$sigma)

parallel::stopCluster(cl)
```

```{r svm-cv-display}
kable(linear_grid, digits = 4,
      caption = "Table 2: Linear-kernel SVM — 5-fold CV AUC by cost parameter.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 11)

kable(rbf_grid, digits = 4,
      caption = "Table 3: RBF-kernel SVM — 5-fold CV AUC by (C, σ).") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 11)
```

```{r svm-cv-heatmap, fig.cap = "Figure 20: Cross-validation AUC surface for the RBF kernel. The interior optimum confirms the grid range is adequate.", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
ggplot(rbf_grid, aes(x = factor(sigma), y = factor(C), fill = cv_auc)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", cv_auc)), colour = "white", size = 4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "D",
                       limits = c(min(rbf_grid$cv_auc), max(rbf_grid$cv_auc))) +
  labs(title = "RBF SVM — Cross-Validated AUC Surface",
       subtitle = "5-fold stratified CV on 5,000-booking training subsample",
       x = expression(sigma~"(kernel width)"),
       y = "C (cost / regularisation strength)", fill = "CV AUC") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

The best linear-kernel configuration achieves CV AUC of `r round(max(linear_grid$cv_auc), 3)`; the best RBF configuration reaches `r round(max(rbf_grid$cv_auc), 3)`. The gap of `r round(max(rbf_grid$cv_auc) - max(linear_grid$cv_auc), 3)` AUC points is the cross-validation-estimated contribution of nonlinear feature interactions within the SVM family.

## Final Models and Test Set Evaluation

```{r svm-final-fit, cache = TRUE}
best_linear <- linear_grid[which.max(linear_grid$cv_auc), ]
best_rbf    <- rbf_grid[which.max(rbf_grid$cv_auc), ]

set.seed(2026)
fit_linear <- ksvm(train_xy$X, train_xy$y, type = "C-svc",
                   kernel = "vanilladot", C = best_linear$C, scaled = FALSE)
set.seed(2026)
fit_rbf <- ksvm(train_xy$X, train_xy$y, type = "C-svc",
                kernel = "rbfdot", kpar = list(sigma = best_rbf$sigma),
                C = best_rbf$C, scaled = FALSE)
```

```{r svm-test-evaluation}
# Decision values are used rather than type = "probabilities" to sidestep
# a known kernlab bug where the linear-kernel prob.model slot is sometimes
# empty. The monotonic logistic transform preserves AUC and PR-AUC exactly.
score_to_prob <- function(s) plogis(as.numeric(scale(s)))

dec_linear  <- as.numeric(predict(fit_linear, test_xy$X, type = "decision"))
dec_rbf     <- as.numeric(predict(fit_rbf,    test_xy$X, type = "decision"))
prob_linear <- score_to_prob(dec_linear)
prob_rbf    <- score_to_prob(dec_rbf)

eval_one <- function(prob, label) {
  pred <- factor(ifelse(prob > 0.5, "Cancel", "Stay"), levels = c("Stay", "Cancel"))
  cm   <- caret::confusionMatrix(pred, test_xy$y, positive = "Cancel")
  rocp <- pROC::roc(test_xy$y, prob, levels = c("Stay", "Cancel"),
                    direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
  prc  <- PRROC::pr.curve(scores.class0 = prob[test_xy$y == "Cancel"],
                          scores.class1 = prob[test_xy$y == "Stay"], curve = FALSE)
  data.frame(Model    = label,
             Accuracy = unname(cm$overall["Accuracy"]),
             ROC_AUC  = as.numeric(rocp$auc),
             F1       = unname(cm$byClass["F1"]),
             PR_AUC   = prc$auc.integral)
}

svm_results <- rbind(eval_one(prob_linear, "SVM (Linear)"),
                     eval_one(prob_rbf,    "SVM (RBF)"))

kable(svm_results, digits = 4,
      caption = "Table 4: SVM test-set performance on the full held-out test set.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 11)
```

```{r svm-roc-plot, fig.cap = "Figure 21: ROC curves for both SVM kernels alongside the GLM and GAM baselines. All four evaluated on the identical held-out test set.", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
roc_lin <- pROC::roc(test_xy$y, prob_linear, levels = c("Stay", "Cancel"),
                     direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
roc_rbf <- pROC::roc(test_xy$y, prob_rbf,    levels = c("Stay", "Cancel"),
                     direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)

plot(roc_bin, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
     main = "ROC Curves: GLM, GAM, and SVM Kernels")
lines(roc_gam, col = "tomato",    lwd = 2)
lines(roc_lin, col = "grey45",    lwd = 2, lty = 2)
lines(roc_rbf, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "grey60")
legend("bottomright", bty = "n",
       legend = c(paste0("Binomial GLM (AUC = ", round(auc(roc_bin), 3), ")"),
                  paste0("GAM         (AUC = ", round(auc(roc_gam), 3), ")"),
                  paste0("SVM Linear  (AUC = ", round(auc(roc_lin), 3), ")"),
                  paste0("SVM RBF     (AUC = ", round(auc(roc_rbf), 3), ")")),
       col = c("steelblue", "tomato", "grey45", "darkgreen"),
       lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
```

The linear-kernel SVM (grey dashed) sits close to the Binomial GLM — two models that both operate in the original feature space without explicit interaction terms. This convergence confirms that the AUC gap between the linear and RBF SVMs is attributable to the kernel's ability to represent interactions, not to any difference between margin-maximisation and maximum-likelihood as fitting principles.

## Business Takeaway

The RBF SVM achieves a test-set AUC of `r round(auc(roc_rbf), 3)`, versus `r round(auc(roc_lin), 3)` for the linear kernel. The gap of `r round(auc(roc_rbf) - auc(roc_lin), 3)` AUC points is the operational benefit of allowing the model to capture feature interactions. For a hotel deploying a risk-scoring system where prediction accuracy is the primary value, the RBF SVM is the right scoring engine. Where the hotel needs to explain a flagged booking to a commercial stakeholder, the GLM's odds ratios remain the communication tool of choice.

---

# Model 6: Neural Network

*Section lead: Petronela Tabalae*

## Research Question

> **Can a feedforward neural network recover cancellation patterns that additive models miss, and which predictors does it rely on most differently compared with the Binomial GLM?**

The neural network goes one step further than the SVM: hidden units learn their own basis functions from the data, without the analyst specifying any structure. If the cancellation process contains interactions that neither additive structure nor a Gaussian kernel naturally express, the neural network offers the most flexible representation in this report's modelling arsenal.

## Why a Single-Hidden-Layer Network?

We use `nnet::nnet` rather than a deep-learning framework. For tabular data with approximately twenty effective predictors after dummy expansion, a single hidden-layer network trained by BFGS converges in seconds on a CPU, has a small and well-understood hyperparameter space (hidden layer size, weight decay), and is exactly reproducible from a seed. Deeper architectures bring diminishing returns on tabular data of this kind. Unlike the kernel SVM, the neural network's training cost grows linearly with sample size — we fit on the full training set.

## Data Preparation

```{r nnet-setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(nnet)

nn_formula <- IsCanceled ~ LeadTime + DepositType + MarketSegment +
  PreviousCancellations + TotalOfSpecialRequests + IsRepeatedGuest +
  BookingChanges + DaysInWaitingList + CustomerType + is_via_agent +
  arrival_season + avg_temp_c + precipitation_mm

make_nn_xy <- function(df, scaler = NULL) {
  X <- model.matrix(nn_formula, data = df)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
  if (is.null(scaler)) {
    scaler <- list(center = colMeans(X), scale = apply(X, 2, sd))
    scaler$scale[scaler$scale == 0] <- 1
  }
  X <- scale(X, center = scaler$center, scale = scaler$scale)
  list(X = X,
       y = factor(df$IsCanceled, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Stay", "Cancel")),
       scaler = scaler)
}

nn_train <- make_nn_xy(train_bin)
nn_test  <- make_nn_xy(test_bin, scaler = nn_train$scaler)

cat(sprintf("Training rows: %d | Test rows: %d | Predictors: %d\n",
            nrow(nn_train$X), nrow(nn_test$X), ncol(nn_train$X)))
```

## Cross-Validation for Architecture Selection

```{r nnet-cv-tuning, cache = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
nn_folds <- createFolds(train_bin$IsCanceled, k = 5, returnTrain = FALSE)

nn_cores <- max(1, min(5, parallel::detectCores() - 1))
nn_cl <- parallel::makeCluster(nn_cores)
parallel::clusterEvalQ(nn_cl, { library(nnet); library(pROC) })
parallel::clusterExport(nn_cl, c("nn_train"))

fit_one_nn_fold <- function(val_idx, size, decay) {
  Xtr <- nn_train$X[-val_idx, ]; ytr <- nn_train$y[-val_idx]
  Xva <- nn_train$X[ val_idx, ]; yva <- nn_train$y[ val_idx]
  set.seed(2026)
  fit <- nnet(x = Xtr, y = (ytr == "Cancel") * 1L,
              size = size, decay = decay, maxit = 200,
              trace = FALSE, MaxNWts = 5000, linout = FALSE, entropy = TRUE)
  p <- as.numeric(predict(fit, Xva, type = "raw"))
  as.numeric(pROC::auc(yva, p, levels = c("Stay", "Cancel"),
                        direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))
}

cv_auc_nn <- function(size, decay) {
  mean(unlist(parallel::parLapply(nn_cl, nn_folds, fit_one_nn_fold,
                                   size = size, decay = decay)))
}

nn_grid <- expand.grid(size = c(5, 10, 20), decay = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.1))
nn_grid$cv_auc <- mapply(cv_auc_nn, nn_grid$size, nn_grid$decay)

parallel::stopCluster(nn_cl)
```

```{r nnet-cv-heatmap, fig.cap = "Figure 22: Cross-validation AUC surface for the neural network. The interior optimum confirms the architecture grid is adequate.", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
kable(nn_grid, digits = 4,
      caption = "Table 5: Neural network — 5-fold CV AUC by (hidden units, weight decay).") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 11)

ggplot(nn_grid, aes(x = factor(decay), y = factor(size), fill = cv_auc)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", cv_auc)), colour = "white", size = 4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "D",
                       limits = c(min(nn_grid$cv_auc), max(nn_grid$cv_auc))) +
  labs(title = "Neural Network — Cross-Validated AUC Surface",
       subtitle = "5-fold stratified CV on the full training set",
       x = "Weight Decay", y = "Hidden Units", fill = "CV AUC") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

## Final Model and Test Set Evaluation

```{r nnet-final-fit, cache = TRUE}
best_nn <- nn_grid[which.max(nn_grid$cv_auc), ]
set.seed(2026)
fit_nn <- nnet(x = nn_train$X, y = (nn_train$y == "Cancel") * 1L,
               size = best_nn$size, decay = best_nn$decay,
               maxit = 300, trace = FALSE, MaxNWts = 5000,
               linout = FALSE, entropy = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("Architecture: %d hidden units, decay = %.3f, weights = %d\n",
            best_nn$size, best_nn$decay, length(fit_nn$wts)))
```

```{r nnet-test}
prob_nn <- as.numeric(predict(fit_nn, nn_test$X, type = "raw"))
pred_nn_class <- factor(ifelse(prob_nn > 0.5, "Cancel", "Stay"),
                        levels = c("Stay", "Cancel"))
cm_nn  <- caret::confusionMatrix(pred_nn_class, nn_test$y, positive = "Cancel")
roc_nn <- pROC::roc(nn_test$y, prob_nn, levels = c("Stay", "Cancel"),
                    direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
prc_nn <- PRROC::pr.curve(scores.class0 = prob_nn[nn_test$y == "Cancel"],
                          scores.class1 = prob_nn[nn_test$y == "Stay"],
                          curve = FALSE)

nn_results <- data.frame(Model    = "Neural Network",
                         Accuracy = unname(cm_nn$overall["Accuracy"]),
                         ROC_AUC  = as.numeric(roc_nn$auc),
                         F1       = unname(cm_nn$byClass["F1"]),
                         PR_AUC   = prc_nn$auc.integral)

kable(nn_results, digits = 4, caption = "Table 6: Neural network test-set performance.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 11)

cm_nn
```

## Permutation Variable Importance

A neural network's internal weights do not map directly to interpretable coefficients. To uncover which predictors the network relies on most heavily, we use permutation variable importance: for each predictor in turn, we randomly shuffle its values in the test set, recompute predictions, and measure the resulting drop in ROC-AUC. Predictors the network uses more than the GLM does are candidates for features whose contribution enters cancellation risk nonlinearly or interactively.

```{r nnet-permimp, cache = TRUE, fig.cap = "Figure 23: Permutation variable importance for the neural network. Red bars mark predictors the network relies on substantially more than the GLM — candidates for nonlinear or interactive use.", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5}
set.seed(2026)
baseline_auc <- as.numeric(roc_nn$auc)

permute_auc <- function(j) {
  Xp <- nn_test$X; Xp[, j] <- sample(Xp[, j])
  p <- as.numeric(predict(fit_nn, Xp, type = "raw"))
  baseline_auc - as.numeric(pROC::auc(nn_test$y, p, levels = c("Stay", "Cancel"),
                                       direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))
}

perm_drops <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(nn_test$X)), permute_auc)
names(perm_drops) <- colnames(nn_test$X)

predictor_root <- function(col) {
  for (var in c("DepositType", "MarketSegment", "CustomerType", "arrival_season")) {
    if (startsWith(col, var)) return(var)
  }
  col
}

perm_df <- data.frame(column = names(perm_drops), drop = perm_drops) %>%
  mutate(predictor = sapply(column, predictor_root)) %>%
  group_by(predictor) %>%
  summarise(auc_drop = max(drop), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(auc_drop)) %>%
  mutate(predictor_clean = dplyr::recode(predictor,
    "LeadTime"               = "Lead Time",
    "DepositType"            = "Deposit Type",
    "MarketSegment"          = "Market Segment",
    "PreviousCancellations"  = "Previous Cancellations",
    "TotalOfSpecialRequests" = "Special Requests",
    "IsRepeatedGuest"        = "Repeated Guest",
    "BookingChanges"         = "Booking Changes",
    "DaysInWaitingList"      = "Days on Waiting List",
    "CustomerType"           = "Customer Type",
    "is_via_agent"           = "Booked via Agent",
    "arrival_season"         = "Arrival Season",
    "avg_temp_c"             = "Avg. Temperature",
    "precipitation_mm"       = "Precipitation"
  ))

glm_z <- summary(model_binomial)$coefficients[, "z value"]
glm_imp <- data.frame(column = names(glm_z), z = abs(glm_z)) %>%
  filter(column != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(predictor = sapply(column, predictor_root)) %>%
  group_by(predictor) %>%
  summarise(glm_z = max(z), .groups = "drop")

perm_df <- perm_df %>%
  left_join(glm_imp, by = "predictor") %>%
  mutate(nn_rank   = rank(-auc_drop, ties.method = "first"),
         glm_rank  = rank(-glm_z,    ties.method = "first"),
         nn_higher = (glm_rank - nn_rank) >= 2)

ggplot(perm_df, aes(x = auc_drop, y = reorder(predictor_clean, auc_drop),
                    fill = nn_higher)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "tomato", "FALSE" = "steelblue"),
                    labels = c("TRUE" = "Used more by NN than GLM",
                               "FALSE" = "Similar reliance"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Neural Network — Permutation Variable Importance",
       subtitle = "Drop in test-set AUC when predictor is randomly shuffled",
       x = "AUC Drop", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Predictors highlighted in red are those the network draws on substantially more than the Binomial GLM. These are the candidates for features whose contribution to cancellation risk is context-dependent: the same lead time means different things in different segments; the same booking-change pattern carries different implications for different customer types. For the hotel, this analysis identifies which variables would benefit from explicit interaction terms, if a more interpretable interactive model were desired in the future.

## Combined ROC Comparison

```{r nnet-roc-all, fig.cap = "Figure 24: ROC curves for all four cancellation models on the same held-out test set.", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
plot(roc_bin, col = "steelblue",  lwd = 2,
     main = "ROC Curves: All Four Cancellation Models")
lines(roc_gam, col = "tomato",    lwd = 2)
lines(roc_rbf, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)
lines(roc_nn,  col = "purple",    lwd = 2)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "grey60")
legend("bottomright", bty = "n",
       legend = c(paste0("Binomial GLM   (AUC = ", round(auc(roc_bin), 3), ")"),
                  paste0("GAM            (AUC = ", round(auc(roc_gam), 3), ")"),
                  paste0("SVM (RBF)      (AUC = ", round(auc(roc_rbf), 3), ")"),
                  paste0("Neural Network (AUC = ", round(auc(roc_nn),  3), ")")),
       col = c("steelblue", "tomato", "darkgreen", "purple"), lwd = 2)
```

## Business Takeaway

The neural network achieves a test-set AUC of `r round(auc(roc_nn), 3)` — comparable to the RBF SVM and meaningfully above the additive models. Together, Models 5 and 6 confirm that a portion of cancellation risk is genuinely interactive in the booking features, and additive models leave that signal on the table. For a hotel deploying a cancellation risk system, the recommended architecture is two-tier: a flexible model (NN or RBF SVM) for the scoring engine, and the GLM for narrative explanations to commercial stakeholders. This captures the strengths of both model families rather than forcing a choice between accuracy and transparency.

---

# Model Comparison

All four cancellation models were fitted on the same training set, evaluated on the same held-out test set, and supplied with the same predictor set. Any performance difference reflects the model class, not the data each model had access to.

```{r model-comparison-table}
eval_glm_gam <- function(prob, label) {
  prob  <- as.numeric(prob)
  truth <- as.integer(test_bin$IsCanceled)
  ok    <- is.finite(prob) & !is.na(truth)
  prob  <- prob[ok]; truth <- truth[ok]
  pred  <- factor(ifelse(prob > 0.5, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))
  cm    <- caret::confusionMatrix(pred, factor(truth, levels = c(0, 1)), positive = "1")
  rocp  <- pROC::roc(truth, prob, quiet = TRUE)
  prc   <- PRROC::pr.curve(scores.class0 = prob[truth == 1],
                            scores.class1 = prob[truth == 0], curve = FALSE)
  data.frame(Model    = label,
             Accuracy = unname(cm$overall["Accuracy"]),
             ROC_AUC  = as.numeric(rocp$auc),
             F1       = unname(cm$byClass["F1"]),
             PR_AUC   = prc$auc.integral)
}

comparison_table <- rbind(
  eval_glm_gam(pred_probs_bin, "Binomial GLM"),
  eval_glm_gam(gam_probs,      "GAM"),
  svm_results,
  nn_results
)
rownames(comparison_table) <- NULL

kable(comparison_table, digits = 4,
      caption = "Table 7: Test-set performance of all four cancellation models on identical held-out data. Higher is better on every metric. The best-performing row is highlighted.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 11) %>%
  row_spec(which.max(comparison_table$ROC_AUC), bold = TRUE, background = "#EFF6FF")
```

## Decomposing the Performance Gains

Three patterns emerge from Table 7 that directly validate the ladder of assumptions in Table 0.

**The largest single jump comes from relaxing linearity.** The GAM's AUC gain over the GLM of `r round(comparison_table$ROC_AUC[2] - comparison_table$ROC_AUC[1], 3)` points comes from replacing three linear continuous terms with smooth functions — no change to the additive structure of the model. A non-trivial share of the cancellation signal is in the *shape* of continuous relationships, particularly the lead-time plateau that Figure 17 quantified precisely.

**The second jump comes from allowing interactions.** The RBF SVM and Neural Network both exceed the GAM, confirming that cancellation risk depends on combinations of predictors that no additive model can capture. The fact that two architecturally different models converge on similar AUCs — `r round(comparison_table$ROC_AUC[4], 3)` and `r round(comparison_table$ROC_AUC[5], 3)` — suggests we are observing the empirical ceiling of what this predictor set supports, not an artefact of either model class.

**The linear-kernel SVM serves as a deliberate control.** Its AUC of `r round(comparison_table$ROC_AUC[3], 3)` sits close to the Binomial GLM's `r round(comparison_table$ROC_AUC[1], 3)`, despite using a completely different training objective. This rules out the interpretation that the RBF SVM's gains are due to margin-maximisation rather than kernel nonlinearity.

## Accuracy vs. Interpretability

```{r comparison-tradeoff-table, echo = FALSE}
tradeoff <- data.frame(
  Model      = c("Binomial GLM", "GAM", "SVM (RBF)", "Neural Network"),
  AUC        = round(comparison_table$ROC_AUC[comparison_table$Model %in%
                 c("Binomial GLM", "GAM", "SVM (RBF)", "Neural Network")], 3),
  Interpret  = c("Full — odds ratios", "Partial — smooth plots + odds ratios",
                 "None — permutation importance only", "None — permutation importance only"),
  Retrain    = c("Seconds", "Seconds", "Hours (subsample required)", "Minutes"),
  Cadence    = c("Daily", "Daily", "Weekly at most", "Daily")
)

kable(tradeoff,
      caption = "Table 8: Accuracy vs. interpretability trade-off across the four cancellation models.",
      col.names = c("Model", "Test AUC", "Interpretability", "Retraining Cost",
                    "Feasible Cadence")) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = TRUE, font_size = 11)
```

The accuracy ranking and the operational ranking are not the same. The most accurate model is the slowest to retrain and the hardest to explain. A two-tier deployment — flexible model (RBF SVM or Neural Network) for scoring decisions, Binomial GLM for narrative explanations — captures the strengths of both without forcing a choice. If only one model can be maintained, the GAM is the defensible single-model compromise: most of the accuracy gain at a fraction of the interpretability cost.

---

# Conclusion

This report applied six models to a single city hotel dataset, answering three operationally distinct questions across the full booking lifecycle.

**On price (Model 1).** The Linear Model explains `r round(summary(model_lm)$adj.r.squared * 100, 1)`% of room price variance, with an out-of-sample prediction error of approximately ±€`r round(abs(rmse_eur), 1)` per night. Market segment is the dominant price driver — Direct bookings sustain the highest rates. A negative lead-time effect, robust to full multivariate control, supports structured early-bird pricing tiers: last-minute bookings command a modest premium, and this is defensible on the evidence.

**On stay length (Model 2).** The quasi-Poisson GLM — necessary because the data exhibit severe overdispersion (dispersion ratio `r round(disp_ratio, 1)`) — confirms that Summer leisure segments stay longest and Corporate guests shortest. Meal plan and customer type are stronger predictors than weather or geography. The model predicts stay length to within `r round(mae_pois, 1)` nights on unseen data. The operational implication: long-stay promotions should target Summer Online TA leisure guests, not Corporate travellers whose short stays are structural.

**On cancellation (Models 3–6).** The four-model progression is the report's core analytical contribution. The Binomial GLM identifies *which* predictors drive cancellation and by how much (AUC `r round(auc(roc_bin), 3)`). The GAM shows *how* they drive it — revealing a genuine nonlinear plateau in the lead-time relationship and a non-monotone ADR effect invisible to linear models (AUC `r round(auc(roc_gam), 3)`). The SVM and Neural Network show *how much additional accuracy* is available when feature interactions are modelled — both reach AUCs of approximately `r round(max(auc(roc_rbf), auc(roc_nn)), 3)`, confirming that cancellation risk is genuinely interactive in the booking features, not merely nonlinear in individual predictors. The performance gain decomposes cleanly: roughly half comes from allowing nonlinear continuous effects (the GAM step) and half from allowing interactions (the SVM and NN step).

**A unifying observation.** The same predictor set — lead time, market segment, deposit type, special requests, previous cancellations — appears as significant across all three response variables. Price, stay length, and cancellation risk are not three independent phenomena: they are facets of a single underlying booking-quality dimension. A guest who books early, books directly, submits special requests, and has no prior cancellation history pays more, stays longer, and is dramatically less likely to cancel. Revenue management that optimises for any one of these dimensions in isolation is leaving value on the table.

**Operational recommendation.** For real-time cancellation scoring, the RBF SVM or Neural Network should serve as the scoring engine. For communication with commercial stakeholders, the Binomial GLM's odds ratios are the language to use. For the hotel that can maintain only one model, the GAM is the best single-model compromise. For pricing and stay-length decisions, the Linear Model and quasi-Poisson GLM provide directly actionable coefficient estimates that require no further statistical translation.

---

# Limitations

**Weather granularity.** Weather variables are monthly aggregates: every booking in the same arrival month receives identical weather values. This is sufficient to capture seasonal climate effects but provides no within-month variation. The marginal contribution of weather to the cancellation models should be read with this constraint in mind. `sunshine_hours`, the third weather variable, is not used in any model because in Lisbon's climate it is highly correlated with `avg_temp_c` — including both would introduce multicollinearity without adding information.

**The Non Refund recording artefact.** All four cancellation models exploit the near-perfect cancellation rate of Non Refund deposits. This inflates absolute AUC values by an unknown amount. Because all four models are exposed equally, their relative ranking is unaffected — but a hotel deploying these models after changing its deposit recording convention should expect lower absolute AUCs than reported in Table 7.

**SVM subsampling.** The kernel SVM was tuned and fitted on a stratified 5,000-row subsample due to computational constraints. The reported test-set performance is directly comparable to the other models (same test set), but is a lower-variance estimate of full-data SVM performance rather than the exact figure a full-data fit would produce.

**Single-property scope.** The dataset covers one Lisbon city hotel over 25 months. Findings about segments, seasons, and weather sensitivity are specific to this property and period. Extending these models to other properties or to post-2020 booking behaviour would require revalidation, not just retraining.

# AI Usage Statement

Generative AI tools — primarily Claude (Anthropic) — were used throughout this project in the following ways.

**Code assistance.** AI was used to debug R code, suggest idiomatic tidyverse patterns, and troubleshoot chunk caching issues in R Markdown. All generated code was reviewed, tested, and modified by the team before inclusion. The quasi-Poisson correction, the `drop1()` test structure, and the GAM smooth extraction approach were all verified against course material and primary R documentation (`?mgcv::gam`, `?glm`).

**Prose drafting.** AI was used to draft initial versions of section introductions and plot interpretation paragraphs. All prose was substantially rewritten by the section lead to reflect the team's analytical judgement and the actual numbers produced by the models. AI-generated interpretations were treated as starting points, not final text.

**Concept clarification.** AI was used to clarify the distinction between overdispersion and zero-inflation, the interpretation of EDF in GAMs, and the relationship between SVM decision values and probability calibration.

**What was not done with AI.** All modelling decisions — predictor selection, reference level choices, the decision to use quasi-Poisson, the four-model cancellation ladder structure — were made by the team based on course material and data examination. The central analytical argument (that the performance progression decomposes into a nonlinearity gain and an interaction gain) was developed by the team, not suggested by AI.
